en: Preface to the *Brief Commentary on the Mahāvaipulya Samantabhadra-bodhicitta-sūtra of Definitive Meaning* By Jin-ziguang-lu-dafu,
Acting Minister of the Secretariat, and Minister of the Department of State Affairs.

Written by Pei Xiu, Vice Director of the Chancellery and Grand Master of the Hall of the Accumulated Worthies: "All things composed of blood and breath must possess consciousness; all that possesses consciousness must share the same essence. This is what is called the truly pure, luminous, and wondrous, the void-penetrating and spiritually pervasive, standing alone and enduring."
This is the fundamental source of all sentient beings, and is therefore called the "Mind-Ground";
this is that which all Buddhas have attained, and is therefore called "Bodhi";
it is the mutual penetration and harmonious integration of all things, and is therefore called the "Dharma-Dhātu."
It is called nirvana because it is eternally tranquil and blissful;
it is called purity because it is neither turbid nor leaking;
it is called suchness because it is neither false nor changing.
Because it is free from faults and transcends all that is non-existent, it is called Buddha-nature;
because it protects the good and wards off evil, it is called *dhāraṇī*;
because it conceals and encompasses all, it is called the Tathāgatagarbha.
Because it transcends the profound and hidden, it is called the Land of Secret Adornment (Guhyasamāja);
because it universally encompasses all virtues in great perfection, illuminates the masses of darkness with its singular radiance, it is called Perfect Enlightenment (Samantabhadra).
In reality, all are but the One Mind.
To turn one's back upon it is to be ordinary; to accord with it is to be a sage.
To be deluded by it is the beginning of birth and death; to awaken to it is the cessation of saṃsāra.
If one seeks them intimately, they are śamatha-vipaśyanā, samādhi, and prajñā;
if one extends and broadens them, they are the six pāramitās and the myriad practices.
When these are drawn forth as wisdom, they then become right wisdom.
Relying [on this] as a cause, it subsequently becomes the true cause;
in reality, they are all one dharma.
To be in perfect enlightenment all day long yet never having experienced perfect enlightenment is the state of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*).
One who seeks to realize perfect enlightenment but has not yet reached the ultimate state of *yuanjue* (perfect awakening) is a bodhisattva;
one who is fully endowed with *yuanjue* and abides in its maintenance is a Tathāgata.

Apart from Perfect Enlightenment, there are no six realms; apart from Perfect Enlightenment, there are no three vehicles; without Perfect Enlightenment, there is no Tathāgata; and with the cessation of Perfect Enlightenment, there is no True Dharma. In reality, all are but a single path.
That which all Buddhas of the three periods have realized is precisely this;
that for which the Tathāgata appeared in the world for the sake of the one great matter is precisely this;
and all the sūtras of the Tripiṭaka and the twelve divisions of scripture are precisely intended to explain this.

However, as the Tathāgata bestowed his teachings, there are manifest and esoteric aspects to the Dharma he pointed out; there are extensive and concise formulations of its principles; there are temporal sequences of priority and posteriority; and there are varying depths according to the capacity of those to whom they were addressed. Were it not for those of superior faculties and perfect wisdom, who could possibly master them all?

Therefore, within the Treasury of Radiance (*Prabhāsa-garbha*), the Tathāgata secretly expounded and clearly manifested [this teaching] for the twelve Great Beings; it was transmitted in depth and spread widely, thereby sealing and confirming this Dharma as the fundamental source of all sutras.
Chan Master Guifeng received the Dharma from Master Daoyuan, a disciple of Nan’i and a direct descendant of Heze Shenhui.
One day, he followed the assembly of monks to a meal at the home of Ren Guan, a local official; occupying a lower seat, he received the scriptures in his turn.
Upon encountering the *Nirvana of Perfect Enlightenment Sutra* (*Yuanjue liao yi*), before he had even finished unrolling the scroll, he was moved to tears by realization.
Returning home, he reported his insight to his teacher, who patted him on the back and said:
"You shall greatly propagate the teaching of the perfect and sudden; it is the Buddhas who have entrusted this sutra to you."

Having received the secret seal of the Southern School and been granted the prophetic prediction of the *Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment*, the Chan Master then perused the Tripitaka of Sūtras and Vinaya, mastered treatises such as the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* and the *Mahāyānaśraddhotpāda-śāstra*, and subsequently reined in his progress at the Dharma-realm of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* and settled in meditative seclusion within the wondrous field of the *Perfect Enlightenment*. Therein he investigated the universal moisture of the "single rain" and exhausted the distinct purports of the five teachings, subsequently composing commentaries and exegeses upon them.

The *Great Commentary* (Dàshū) in three fascicles and the *Great Sub-commentary* (Dàchão) in thirteen fascicles; the *Abridged Commentary* (Lüshū) in two fascicles and the *Small Sub-commentary* (Xiǎochão) in six fascicles; and the *Ritual for Cultivation and Realization in the Dharma Hall* (Dàochāng Xiūzhèng Yí) in eighteen fascicles—all of these are currently in circulation throughout the world.

His exposition of the teachings is perfect; his vision of the Dharma is penetrating; his elucidation of meanings is as precise as splitting firewood; and his entry into contemplation is as clear as holding a torch.
Their discourse reaches the ultimate limit of principle and does not indulge in empty flights;
their style supports the teachings and does not employ artifice for its own sake.
They do not disparage others on account of their own strengths, and thus they harbor no polemical assertions of exclusion.
Because he did not use his own lack of attainment to disparage others, he was free from the narrow-minded speculations of the breast.

Vast and expansive, it is truly the eye of the twelve divisions of the scriptures, the marrow of the thirty-five patriarchs, the fundamental root of all living beings, and the universal path of the three periods of time.
Even if there were authors in later generations, they could not surpass this work.
Is it one of the four reliances?
Or is it something heard directly from the Pure Land?
How can its meaning and essence be fully exhausted in such [a manner]!
Someone said:
"The Dao is formless; no one who looks can behold it."
The Way has no fixed direction, and no practitioner can reach its limit.
How much less so can it be captured by written words?
It resides simply within one's own nature; how could it be fully explained by a mere few tens of thousands of characters!
He replied, "Alas! This is not sufficient to speak of the Way."
Did I not say previously:
"That which unifies all virtues in great completeness and illuminates the multitude of delusions with solitary brilliance is Perfect Enlightenment (Yuanjue).
Indeed, Perfect Enlightenment can give rise to all phenomena, yet no phenomenon has ever been apart from Perfect Enlightenment."
Now, as for the texts of the Tripiṭaka—Sūtra, Vinaya, and Abhidharma—that have been transmitted to China, numbering more than five thousand fascicles, what do they expound?
They expound nothing other than precepts, meditative concentration, and wisdom.
What is it that one seeks by cultivating precepts, meditative concentration, and wisdom?
It is none other than Perfect Enlightenment.
Perfect Enlightenment is a single dharma; why then do they seek it by manifesting myriad practices?
The faculties and capacities of sentient beings vary.
Nevertheless, the entire Great Canon consists of sutras on Perfect Enlightenment, and this commentary is a commentary upon that Great Canon.
To unravel the texts of five thousand fascicles with a commentary of only a few scrolls—is this not exceedingly concise!
Why is it said to be so complex?

When one cuts off the path of speech, brings to rest the mind of conceptual thought, forgets the subject and object of cognition, and extinguishes all mental images, only then is attainment realized; it certainly does not reside in verbal expression.
"Alas! The realms through which sentient beings wander are the six paths. Ghosts and spirits suffer the bitterness of deep obscurity and sorrow;

birds and beasts harbor the grief of flight and panic; asuras are consumed by anger; and the various heavens are fixed in pleasure. Only the human path is capable of rectifying the mind and inclining one toward Bodhi."
"If a person does not practice, there is nothing I can do for them.

Having entered the threshold of Master Xiuchang’s realm and received the master’s manifest instructions, I have no way to repay his kindness; I shall simply praise his Dharma directly and announce it to the great assembly. All other details are fully contained in the original preface.

Preface to the *Mahāvaipulya Tathāgatagarbha-parivarta-bodhimaṇḍa-lakṣaṇa-sūtra* (The Scripture on the Perfect Enlightenment of the Great Vaipulya), Explaining the Definitive Meaning, composed by the Śramaṇa Zongmi of Cōngtáng Monastery on Mount Zhōngnán in the Tang Dynasty. “Yuan, Heng, Li, and Zhen” are the virtues of Qian, originating from the single qi.
Permanence, bliss, self, and purity are the virtues of the Buddha, rooted in the single mind.
By concentrating the vital energy one attains pliancy; by cultivating the single mind one accomplishes the Way.

As for this mind: it is profound, empty, wondrous, and pure; it is radiant, brilliant, and spiritually luminous. It neither departs nor arrives, darkly penetrating the three periods of time; it is neither within nor without, penetratingly illuminating the ten directions.
Neither extinguished nor born, how could the four mountains cause harm?
Detached from nature and detached from form, how could the five colors blind one?
Dwelling within the flow of birth and death, the black pearl shines alone amidst the vast blue sea.
Seated upon the shore of nirvana, the cassia moon shines solitary and bright against the azure sky.
How great it is! It is the source from which the myriad dharmas derive their beginning.
The myriad dharmas are illusory and false, arising through the convergence of conditions.
The nature of arising phenomena is fundamentally non-existent; all is but consciousness.
Consciousness is like an illusion or a dream, yet it is simply the one mind.
The mind is quiescent yet cognizant; this is termed Perfect Enlightenment (Yuanjue). It is all-pervading and pure, with no room for anything else within it.
Therefore, its virtuous functions are boundless, yet they are all of one single nature.
The nature arises as phenomena, and the object and wisdom are distinct and clear.
When phenomena attain the nature, they merge in harmony; body and mind become vast and open.
Compared to the Sea-Seal Samādhi, it transcends the great void—vast and resplendent, far beyond the reach of thought and deliberation.
Our Buddha, having realized this, took pity on sentient beings who were deluded by it; he sighed again in wonder at its marvel and contemplated the Great Matter thrice.
Having perfected the Ten Powers, he was able to crush the demonic armies beneath the tree;
thereupon, giving rise to the Four Minds, he desired to reveal the treasure trove within the house.

However, while losing one's head is easy, regaining it and abandoning one's father is difficult; thus, at the Immortal Garden and the Site of Enlightenment, the teachings were established as sudden and gradual.
In the gradual approach, five distinct periods were set forth, with emptiness and existence alternating in their manifestation;
in the sudden approach, there is no distinction between the two truths, for the profound spirit is beyond all dependence.
This present sutra belongs to the category of the sudden teaching!
Thus, when the Tathāgata enters the Land of Tranquil Light, ordinary beings and sages become one source; he manifests the Body of Enjoyment, where the principal and the retinue assemble together.
The Great Being Mañjuśrī first inquired about the cause of the original arising, and the Bhagavān, the Most Honored One, first set forth the ultimate fruit.
Illuminating this true essence, one extinguishes those dream-like forms; knowing there is no self or person, who is it that undergoes saṃsāra?
The various illusory transformations arise from the awakened mind; when illusions are exhausted, awakening is perfected, the mind becomes pervasive, and the Dharma is universal.
The mind is originally the Buddha, yet it drifts and sinks due to the arising of thoughts;
the shore truly does not move, yet it seems to rush past because the boat is traveling.
Suddenly eliminating the false ruler, the void no longer gives rise to flowers;
gradually exhausting the source of craving, gold is freed from its heavy ore.

In principle, there is nothing to be cultivated or realized, yet wisdom appears to have gradations: as one recognizes the errors of each preceding stage, they are designated as successive levels. How much more so for one who has forgotten the arising and ceasing of delusions, whose virtues are equal to perfect luminosity!
Yet, when a fine steed emerges from the stable, it already responds to the mere flicker of the whip;
and when a great treasure is buried in dust, one must devise a method for its recovery.
Thus, when the three contemplations are clarified and made lucid, both the provisional and the ultimate truths are entered.
The various wheels interlace, alternating between single and double, circular and elongated.
The four marks subtly merge with the spirit; there is no awareness that opposes or rejects them.
The four maladies emerge from the body, and the mind-flower radiates its brilliance.
Furthermore, by practicing with long, medium, and short-term commitments, maintaining mindfulness, and restraining the mind through application;
and by training alternately and universally in both specific and general practices, the obstacles of karma and the obstacles of afflictions will be eliminated.
Having accomplished the body of wisdom, with stillness reaching its ultimate limit and awakening pervading everywhere, the Buddha-realm manifests before one across hundreds of thousands of worlds.
Therefore, hearing these five names surpasses the merit of bestowing jewels upon lands;
explaining the meaning of even half a verse excels that of the Hinayana teachings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
In truth, there is not a single dharma that is not upheld, nor a single capacity that is not reached.
Alas! When the folk songs of Ba are harmonized with the multitude, the semblance of wisdom soars upon the monkey-like minds.
The "Snow Song" (the *Vajracchedikā*) must have been rare; the definitive meaning was hidden within the Dragon Treasury.

Zongmi devoted himself exclusively to the ancient Chinese classics, yet he sought the pinnacle of understanding in the Indian scriptures; both were submerged in the trap of expedient means, tasting only the dregs.
Fortunately, on the banks of the Fu River, the needle and the magnet met: Chan encountered the Southern School, and the Teachings encountered this very scripture.
Under a single word, the mind-ground was opened and unobstructed;
within a single scroll, the sky of meaning shone with brilliance.
Recently, I have realized that the Way is not a fixed way, and that all conditioned phenomena are impermanent.
Now, knowing that this mind is the Buddha-mind, one will certainly become a Buddha.

However, since the Buddha is called the One of All-Knowledge (Sarvajña), and because cultivation relies upon extensive learning, he traveled again to a hundred cities to sit and explore the various scriptures.
Although my lectures may be overly grandiose, my learning is modeled after that of Master An.
Having unworthily received the inclusion of the Tathāgata, I have mistakenly been granted the seal of a true disciple.
Meeting my kinsmen and friends once again, I am moved all the more by the Buddha’s grace.
Long have I lamented my solitary poverty and intended to present this Dharma-gift:
I have gathered the Prajñāpāramitā, woven the Avataṃsaka into a continuous thread, extracted the essentials of the Vinaya, and elucidated the Vijñaptimātratā.
Yet among the myriad prescriptions of medical arts, one must select those that provide a specific remedy;
among the thousand treasures of the sea, one first seeks the wish-fulfilling gem.
Observing its wealth of phrasing and breadth of meaning, it truly yields to the *Saṃpuṣpita* (Flower Garland) Sūtra.
Pointing directly to the essence and responding to the occasion, there is nothing that does not accord with Perfect Enlightenment.
Therefore, I have thoroughly examined various treatises and repeatedly studied the works of a hundred schools to sharpen my faculties; only then have I composed this commentary.

With a mind focused on the sagely intent, he applied his utmost thought and refined his studies; the meaning encompasses both *dharmatā* (nature) and *lakṣaṇa* (phenomena), while the meditation includes both sudden and gradual approaches. He has compiled these into three fascicles to transmit to those of diligent learning.
However, as for the superior, middling, and inferior grades, their faculties, desires, and natures differ.

Now, in order to model myself after those [teachings] to bring about completion, I shall follow what is easy and simple, further extract the essential points, and provide a direct commentary on the root scripture, so that one may realize phenomena as mind and achieve daily increase and daily decrease.
Preface to the Sutra on the Definitive Meaning of the Cultivation of Perfect Enlightenment in the Vaipulya Mahāvaipulya Scripture.
